## The Darboux Integral

### Narrative

- §8.1 showed the axioms can force the value of an integral — we define integrability to mean exactly this
- A function is integrable if and only if its value is forced: sup L = inf U
- This is the minimal integral: we declare a function integrable precisely when the axioms leave no choice
- We then verify this definition actually satisfies the three axioms — so the integral exists
- Payoff: continuous functions are integrable (already proved), and so are some discontinuous ones

### Content

**The Minimal Integral**
- Idea: §8.1 ended with a question — does an integral satisfying the axioms exist? We build one.
- Strategy: declare a function integrable when the axioms force its value, and define the integral to be that forced value
- Definition: lower integral = sup_P L(f, P), upper integral = inf_P U(f, P)
- Definition: f is *integrable* on [a,b] if the lower and upper integrals are equal. The common value is ∫_{[a,b]} f.
- Remark: for continuous functions, §8.1 already showed sup L = inf U — so continuous functions are integrable under this definition
- Remark: this is the Darboux integral

**Refinements**
- Definition: a partition Q *refines* P if P ⊆ Q
- Lemma (Refinements Improve Bounds): if P ⊆ Q, then L(f, P) ≤ L(f, Q) ≤ U(f, Q) ≤ U(f, P)
- Proof: add one point at a time; splitting a subinterval can only improve inf/sup estimates
- Corollary: every lower sum ≤ every upper sum (take common refinement P ∪ Q)
- Corollary: lower integral ≤ upper integral

**Verification of the Axioms**
- Theorem: the Darboux integral satisfies all three axioms
- Verify (I1) Rectangles: for constant c, every partition gives L = U = c(b−a)
- Verify (I2) Monotonicity: f ≤ g ⟹ inf/sup on each subinterval respects this ⟹ L(f,P) ≤ L(g,P), so sup L(f) ≤ sup L(g)
- Verify (I3) Additivity: partitions of [a,b] containing c split into partitions of [a,c] and [c,b]; sup over product = sum of sups
- Remark: the integral exists — the forced value actually defines an integral satisfying the axioms

**Beyond Continuous Functions**
- The Darboux definition applies to any bounded function with sup L = inf U
- Theorem: bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities are integrable
- Proof sketch: enclose discontinuities in intervals of small total length; on the rest, uniform continuity controls U − L
- Theorem (exercise): monotone functions on [a,b] are integrable
- Remark: we don't belabor integrability criteria here — a fuller picture comes with the Lebesgue integral
- ✎ Inline: explain why the Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not integrable
